rationale: This mixed-methods household monitoring study (N=17 purposively stratified connected households followed for 180 days from November 2014 to April 2015 in Campina Grande, Brazil) examines how household income (determining domestic tank/cistern storage capacity) and physical hydraulic position in the supply network (topographic elevation and distance from reservoirs) shape the impacts of drought-induced utility water rationing (36-hour weekly scheduled supply suspension) on domestic water storage, per capita consumption, shortage hours, carrying burden, and household hygiene routines. Although background sections briefly mention federal-versus-state water-resource management over the Boqueirão reservoir, the empirical analysis tests socioeconomic and hydraulic-engineering determinants under operational drought rationing rather than any legal or administrative rule-type mechanism from the nine mechanism families (NONE_NO_RULE_MECHANISM). Outcomes center squarely on service continuity/shortage hours, water consumption quantity, domestic storage/water quality, and physical water-carrying burden (effective_access).
